chapter: Big bands, Depression work and the WPA band
title: The WPA band
summary: Ernie explains the rule that kept him out of the WPA band, the huge number of players and tests that weeded out poor readers. The band played at schools, hospitals and parades.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: The Depression years and the WPA band

blocks.x: Crab. Just give it to you like that. I'm telling you. In the Depression, the men that belong to these big bands, they weren't in that WPA band then.

Oh yeah. All in the same band? Both of them. The majority of them, matter of fact, when the WPA band Frey started, the men that could play music wasn't working like out in City Park where they were digging those lagoon or anything. They had registered to play music, but this was the thing. You couldn't have over two or three in one family in the same profession that could get in that band, you see. Now, see, when my- I wasn't married, so when my brother got in the band, I couldn't get him because, see, he told his people he was taking care of me and him too. So that got me out and I couldn't get in. And actually, I'll show you how many musicians they had in it.
I'll take a picture of it, great big people.
Yeah. The same boy you call Edward Johnson, Alessa Santiago, he was the 52nd alto player in the band.
That's how many alto players, and you see where Jackson Square is. The snare drum was set against the fence from that end all the way on the other end. There was nothing but snare drum players.
My committee tried to get me equipped me in that band.

Everybody could play the instrument was in that band. Well, you see, after they start ironing them out and bringing them before the board and testing them out, well, they ironed them out, you and broke them on those that couldn't actually start reading those heavy marshes and things, well, they put them back in the field. Unless they were sick to certain extent, they would give them an easier job.
If it was, they couldn't read them, they had to go back.

Well, quite naturally, they had to go back in the field. Of course, when they first started, they just went out there and played anything they wanted, and they bring them out in the neutral ground, Claiborne Street around 2 o'clock in the evening, for when school would open, and all the children come from school, they would enjoy it, you see. Then they'd bring them to the jailhouse and to the hospitals and play for the sick, you know, and different places like that.
Yeah, they did this real good.
Yeah, like Holiday's and the parade on Canal Street, they'd be 20 blocks long, just that one band. Yeah, right across the river. Have them holding the hogs, you know.
Biggest band I ever seen. I couldn't get in it.

The committees tried to make me go in that band. They said, we need men like you in that band. But I'm going to stand right here where I'm at. I was playing at the Crystal Palace with an all-day pastor at that particular time at night. And I had, I was on the WP in the day. I was doing all right. I was waiting with the commission here on Sunday. The telly order. Yeah.
